title: The Transfer Window
primary_metric: kilograms of payload deliverable per day of transit time

options.A: The Direct Burn — a high-thrust, direct parametric transfer trajectory that reaches the target orbit fastest, at the cost of a higher propellant mass fraction
options.B: The Patient Drift — a low-thrust, extended-coast parametric transfer trajectory that preserves more deliverable payload mass, at the cost of longer radiation exposure in transit

sources.claim: Firefly Aerospace's Sherpa orbital transfer vehicle product line (formerly Spaceflight Inc.'s Sherpa OTVs) is a real, currently-offered rideshare-to-orbit product family, comprising the chemical-bipropellant Sherpa-LTC and the electric-propulsion Sherpa-LTE variants

sources.title: Firefly Aerospace acquires Spaceflight Inc.
sources.note: Confirms Firefly continues operating the Sherpa OTV line post-acquisition, i.e. it is a currently-offered product, not a discontinued one.

sources.claim: Sherpa-LTC's published wet mass and its flown parking-orbit altitude
sources.value: 180 kg wet mass; 500 km Sun-synchronous parking orbit
sources.title: Sherpa-LTC 1, 2
sources.note: Secondary aggregator (not the manufacturer), but a well-regarded, detailed one. No dry mass is published for a bus flying either propulsion mode generically -- see MA4 in Appendix E. Tier 2 probe 6 (2026-08-31) confirmed both cited figures are real page content but flagged that they describe two distinct flown Sherpa-LTC units rather than one unified spec (180 kg wet mass is unit #2's figure; 500 km SSO is unit #1's flown orbit) -- both are real, on-page Sherpa-LTC figures for the same vehicle family/product line this case models generically (SEE APPENDIX A/G), not a single flight's complete spec sheet; case.md does not claim otherwise.

sources.claim: Sherpa-LTE's Hall-effect thruster specific impulse, total delta-v capability, and parking orbit

sources.title: Sherpa-LTE
sources.note: Delta-v figure is the vehicle's stated total propulsive capability, used here as the Patient Drift's transfer delta-v budget; checked against general low-thrust LEO-GEO transfer literature and found consistent in order of magnitude (see RESEARCH_LOG.md Key Finding #1).

sources.claim: Geostationary orbit altitude above Earth's surface
sources.title: Orbits — Earth Observation Data Basics (NASA Earthdata)
sources.note: Combined with S5's Earth radius to get GEO radius-from-center (Appendix A).

sources.title: Earth radius
sources.note: Secondary source for a standard, uncontested geodetic constant. Used to convert both the parking-orbit and GEO altitudes into radii-from-center.

sources.org: Wikipedia (citing the WGS84 geocentric gravitational constant, NIMA TR8350.2)
sources.title: Standard gravitational parameter
sources.note: Tier 2 probe 6 (2026-08-31) found the previously-cited NAIF geophysical.ker kernel file does not literally contain 398,600.4418 (it lists 398600.8 for WGS72 and 398600.5 for WGS84 instead) -- a live-but-drifted citation, corrected here. 398,600.4418 km^3/s^2 is the WGS84-adopted geocentric gravitational constant (NIMA TR8350.2, 1994 update), confirmed live on this Wikipedia page's summary table (3.986004418(8)x10^14 m^3/s^2, Earth row). Used with S4/S5's radii in the standard two-body Hohmann-transfer equations to derive the Direct Burn's semi-major axis, eccentricity, delta-v, and transit time (see the Appendix B footnote in case.md for the full derivation).

sources.claim: Specific impulse of the Ocelot HTP/octane bipropellant thruster, the engine installed on Sherpa-LTC
sources.title: Qualification Testing of a High-Performance 22N Bipropellant Thruster Using HTP + Octane
sources.note: Manufacturer's own published figure. 22 N thrust matches Sherpa-LTC's stated 4x22N thruster configuration (S2), confirming this is the Direct Burn's chemical mode engine.

sources.claim: Commercial all-electric-propulsion GEO satellites (e.g. Boeing 702SP) fly GTO-to-GEO solar-electric-propulsion transfers on the order of 6 months
sources.title: All-Electric (satellite propulsion overview)
sources.note: Real commercial precedent that customers accept ~6-month electric orbit-raising windows today. Used as the anchor for both MA1 (contract delivery window) and MA3 (Patient Drift transit time).

sources.claim: Electric orbit raising to GEO can take up to 200 days, versus a few days for conventional chemical propulsion, and this extended Van Allen belt transit is a documented radiation-exposure risk
sources.org: Royal Astronomical Society (reporting Lozinski et al., Space Weather)
sources.title: Space weather causes years of radiation damage to satellites using electric propulsion
sources.note: Reports Lozinski et al. 2019, 'Solar Cell Degradation due to Proton Belt Enhancements During Electric Orbit Raising to GEO,' Space Weather, DOI 10.1029/2019SW002213 — a real peer-reviewed paper, verified via this primary institutional press release. Corroborates S8's transit-time order of magnitude and establishes that slow electric transits carry a documented, real radiation-exposure cost distinct from a simple linear dose-rate model.

sources.claim: A currently-available commercial small-satellite bus's published total-ionizing-dose radiation tolerance
sources.title: All of the M6P nano-satellite bus subsystems found to be radiation tolerant to 20krad, after the product qualification tests
sources.note: Manufacturer's own qualification-test figure, but qualified against a worst-case 5-year LEO mission, not a GEO-transfer profile specifically. Used as a real, currently-available proxy for Appendix A's payload tolerance since no public GEO-transfer-specific figure was found for a comparably-sized commercial payload.

sources.claim: Real altitude ranges of Earth's inner and outer Van Allen radiation belts
sources.title: Earth's plasmasphere and the Van Allen belts (Cluster mission)
sources.note: Combined with Appendix A's real parking-orbit and GEO radii to derive that belt-radius territory covers approximately 48% of the radial distance of the LEO-to-GEO climb (both belts overlap most, but not all, of the transfer range — there is a real 'slot' region of much lower flux between them). Used identically for both options since both cross the same physical belts between the same two radii; see the derived entry below.

sources.claim: Direct Burn semi-major axis, eccentricity, delta-v, and idealized ballistic transit time, computed from S4-S6 via the standard two-body Hohmann-transfer equations
sources.value: a=24,521 km; e=0.7195; delta-v=3.82 km/s; transit time=0.221 days (5.3 hr)
sources.title: Hohmann transfer computation from Appendix A radii and S6's GM
sources.note: a=(r1+r2)/2; e=(r2-r1)/(r2+r1); delta-v1 and delta-v2 from the vis-viva equation at each radius; transit time is half the transfer ellipse's Keplerian period, T=2*pi*sqrt(a^3/mu). This is an idealized single-burn ballistic coast time; it excludes real burn duration and mission-ops margin, which is disclosed in case.md.

sources.claim: Propellant mass for each option, derived from the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation using each option's sourced/derived delta-v and Isp against the sourced wet mass
sources.value: Direct Burn 133.0 kg (73.9% of wet mass); Patient Drift 63.7 kg (35.4% of wet mass)
sources.title: Propellant-mass-fraction computation from Appendix B delta-v/Isp and Appendix C wet mass
sources.note: mass fraction = 1 - exp(-delta-v/(Isp*g0)), g0=9.80665 m/s^2. Cross-checked against real chemical (3-4:1) vs Hall-effect (1.3-1.5:1) mass-ratio literature found during research and found consistent in order of magnitude.

sources.claim: Fraction of the LEO-to-GEO radial climb spent within Van Allen belt-radius territory, derived from S11's real belt altitudes and Appendix A's real parking/GEO radii
sources.title: Belt-crossing-fraction computation
sources.note: Radial-distance fraction used as a proxy for time fraction; real speed varies along each trajectory (much faster near periapsis than apoapsis for the Direct Burn's ellipse), so true time-in-belt fraction could differ from this radial approximation. Disclosed as a simplification in case.md. Same value used for both options since both cross the same physical belts between the same two radii (see MA2).

_ext: keys below are pipeline extensions, additive to SPEC §4
protagonist: Talia Brooks, Trajectory Analyst, Meridian Launch Systems

deliverables.text: A pair of parametric position equations, x(E) and y(E), for each trajectory option (the Direct Burn and the Patient Drift), using each option's stated semi-major axis and eccentricity from Appendix B, with the parameter identified by name and explained in plain terms (what it represents physically, and what values it ranges over for one full transfer).

For each option, the rectangular (Cartesian) equation of the trajectory's path, found by eliminating the parameter from that option's D1 equations, showing every algebraic step — followed by a solved check, using that rectangular equation, of the point where each trajectory actually reaches Appendix A's target orbit radius, with your algebra shown in full.

A propellant-mass-fraction and deliverable-payload-mass calculation for each option, using the kick stage's fixed total wet mass and dry mass and each option's stated propellant load from Appendix C, with every percent calculated shown as arithmetic, not just stated as a result.

A single primary-metric comparison table — kilograms of deliverable payload per day of transit time, for both options — built from your D2 transit-time figures and your D3 deliverable-payload-mass figures, with the division shown for each option.

A cumulative radiation-dose estimate for each option's payload, using Appendix D's dose-rate reference and each option's own transit time (from D2) and belt-crossing duration, with your unit conversions shown explicitly and both results compared against Appendix A's stated payload radiation tolerance limit.
A recommendation to the payload customer, defended using your D4 and D5 results, stating plainly what would have to change about the transfer design for your recommendation to flip.

appendices.title: Van Allen Belt Radiation Dose Reference

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: MA1's 240-day contract delivery window is anchored to real commercial precedent (S8: ~6-month/180-day all-electric GTO-GEO transfers), set some headroom above the Patient Drift's own modeled 180-day transit. Tier 2 probe 5 reports this dial as breaking the 20% cap under both +/-50% flex, but that is a restatement of the case's own MCS-46-waived baseline margin (~15,940% before any flex, per case.json.balance_test_waiver), not a new instability MA1 introduces. The one real, disclosed effect: flexing MA1 down to 120 days makes the Patient Drift's real 180-day transit exceed the window outright, disqualifying it on the delivery-window gate independent of the kg/day metric -- exactly what case.md Appendix E's own MA1 sensitivity note already states ('below 180 days, the Patient Drift becomes contractually unflyable outright'). Flexing MA1 up to 360 days changes nothing (the window already never binds either option above ~200 days, per the same note).

MA3 (the Patient Drift's 180-day transit time) is the single largest lever in the whole comparison and is deliberately the most heavily re-verified figure in the case (see RESEARCH_LOG.md's 'RETUNE PASS' -- confirmed to sit inside real Boeing 702SP-class all-electric GEO-transfer precedent, not at an inflated extreme). Tier 2 probe 5 reports this dial as breaking the 20% cap under both +/-50% flex: -50% (90 days) narrows the margin to ~7,916% (the Direct Burn still wins by roughly 80x); +50% (270 days) exceeds MA1's 240-day delivery window and disqualifies the Patient Drift outright (its reported ~7,684% margin figure is a formula artifact of dividing against a zero-feasibility baseline, per SKILL.md's documented P5 zero-baseline caveat, not a real percentage). Every direction tested either narrows the gap without closing it or removes the Patient Drift from contention entirely -- consistent with sensitivity_model.py's own finding that no real value of MA3 brings the margin under SPEC's ~20% cap.

MA4 (30 kg dry mass) has no public source -- no published figure exists for a single bus flying both a chemical and an electric mode at this delta-v/Isp combination -- and is the case's own most-flagged unsourced figure (case.md Appendix E's own MA4 sensitivity note: 'major lever... raising dry mass shrinks both options' payload roughly linearly, narrowing but not closing the kg/day gap'). Tier 2 probe 5 confirms exactly that: -50% (15 kg) widens the margin to ~25,621%; +50% (45 kg) narrows it to ~2,164%, still two orders of magnitude outside the cap and no flip. This is the case's own documented, disclosed sensitivity finding restated by the probe, not a new discovery.

MA5 (50 rad/day) feeds only the D5 radiation-dose pass/fail check against Appendix A's 20,000-rad tolerance limit, a separate constraint from the primary D4 kg/day metric -- flexing it +/-50% (25 or 75 rad/day) leaves both options' cumulative dose (roughly 2,160-6,480 rad for the Patient Drift, well under tolerance either way) comfortably passing, so it correctly does not move margin_pct at all. Tier 2 probe 5's report that this 'breaks the 20% cap' is the same restated MCS-46-waived baseline margin appearing at every flex value of a dial that structurally cannot touch it, not a genuine instability.

Anchors 2-3 combine into one pass; the two deep-conflict threads (ratio-dominance compounding; what a real flip would require) run as a single combined thread instead of two; total runtime shortens to roughly 30 minutes, content held constant.

derived.sensitivity_note: sensitivity_model.py (run 2026-08-31): base margin ~15,931% (matches case.json.margin_pct=15,940.5 to within rounding -- the case's own figures round the rocket-equation outputs to 17.0/86.3/133.0/63.7 kg before dividing; the model carries full precision). MA3 (Patient Drift transit time) flexed toward MA1's 240-day contract ceiling (239 days) WIDENS the margin to ~21,186%; flexed past that ceiling (270+ days) disqualifies the Patient Drift outright on the MA1 delivery-window gate. MA4 (dry mass) flexed to 45 kg (+50%) shrinks both options' payload but does not change the winner. MA1 (delivery window) flexed down to 120 days disqualifies the Patient Drift outright (its real 180-day transit exceeds it), independent of the kg/day metric. Every flex tested either widens the Direct Burn's win or disqualifies the Patient Drift outright -- none narrows the gap toward parity, let alone flips it. What-would-have-to-change figure (FACILITATOR.md Deep Conflict thread 2): closing the ~76.84-vs-0.479 kg/day gap to parity requires the Patient Drift's transit time to shrink to roughly 1.1 days (86.28 kg / 76.84 kg/day) -- near-chemical speed, at which point it would no longer describe a real low-thrust electric transfer.
derived.facilitator_ratio_terms_note: Facilitator-only rounded terms used throughout FACILITATOR.md's narrative (Twist, Socratic questions, Deep Conflict): payload-mass ratio approximately 5.1x (Patient Drift ahead, 86.3/17.0); transit-time ratio approximately 815x (Direct Burn ahead, 180/0.221); resulting D4 kg/day ratio approximately 160x (76.9/0.479, equivalently the case.json.margin_pct=15,940.5 percent figure); MA3 flexed to 239 days widens that ratio further, to approximately 21,000 percent (21,186%, see sensitivity_model.py). All four rounded figures are direct restatements of case.json.balance.margin_basis and this derived object's sensitivity_note, kept here as an explicit cross-reference so FACILITATOR.md's narrative figures are checkable against case.json rather than free-floating.
derived.twist_additive_score_note: sensitivity_model.py's evaluate_twist() illustrates the FACILITATOR.md Twist: an evenly-weighted (50/50) additive score built from each option's payload-mass fraction (of wet mass) and a normalized speed fraction (transit time inverted and scaled against the slower option) gives the Direct Burn approximately 0.547 and the Patient Drift approximately 0.240 -- the Direct Burn still wins under this alternate, equally-legitimate metric construction. Unlike The Phasing Call (where an analogous additive reconstruction flips the winner), this case's speed asymmetry (~815x) is large enough on its own that no additive reconstruction with real inputs credibly closes the gap, let alone flips it. This is itself a finding worth stating to a room: not every landslide margin is an artifact of the ratio construction -- some are real regardless of how the two real quantities are combined.

balance_test_waiver.reason: Per MCS-46: the margin (15,940.5%) is real, honestly researched, and structurally driven, not a modeling shortcut -- confirmed by a dedicated retune pass (RESEARCH_LOG.md, 'RETUNE PASS -- 2026-08-31') that checked and ruled out both the two most likely artifacts (MA3's 180-day transit time being an unrealistic extreme; a different primary metric closing the gap without fabricating a number). Waived because (1) the setup still forces genuine multi-step analytical work -- deriving each option's transfer ellipse and rectangular equation from real orbital radii, computing each option's propellant-mass fraction via the rocket equation from real Isp/delta-v figures, and combining deliverable-payload-mass with transit-time into a single kg/day ratio is not a plug-and-chug exercise -- and (2) the size of the gap is not guessable from the premise alone: the premise only supports the well-known qualitative fact that chemical propulsion is faster and electric propulsion is more propellant-efficient, not the specific magnitudes, and a student's naive intuition (a much-more-efficient electric engine should plausibly bank enough extra payload mass to be worth its extra months in transit, the same way the case's own Argument B frames it) is actively wrong until the real ~800x transit-time asymmetry (a structural consequence of chemical thrust running in newtons-to-kilonewtons versus Hall-effect electric thrust in millinewtons) is computed and shown to swamp the real but comparatively modest ~5x payload-mass asymmetry the rocket equation actually produces -- discovering that the two asymmetries are not remotely the same order of magnitude, and that the metric's ratio construction lets the larger one dominate completely, is itself the pedagogical payoff. Per project owner: scoped narrowly to this case's own researched figures, not a general relaxation, and not retroactive to any other case.

balance.argument_a: The Direct Burn reaches geostationary orbit in a modeled 0.221 days (about 5.3 hours) against the Patient Drift's modeled 180 days (Appendix B) — a real transit-time advantage of roughly 815x, driven by the underlying physics of chemical thrust (newtons-to-kilonewtons) versus Hall-effect electric thrust (millinewtons). Delivering 17.0 kg of payload (180 kg wet mass minus 30 kg dry mass minus 133.0 kg propellant, Appendix C) in 0.221 days works out to roughly 76.9 kg of deliverable payload per day of transit — comfortably inside Talia's contracted 240-day delivery window (Appendix A) with almost two full orders of magnitude of schedule margin to spare, and a real, contracted value the customer is already paying for.
balance.argument_b: The Patient Drift's electric propulsion needs a larger delta-v budget for the same transfer (6.0 km/s versus the Direct Burn's 3.82 km/s, Appendix B) but its far higher specific impulse (1,400 s versus 290 s) still converts that into only 63.7 kg of propellant, versus the Direct Burn's 133.0 kg — leaving 86.3 kg of deliverable payload (180 kg wet mass minus 30 kg dry mass minus 63.7 kg propellant, Appendix C), roughly 5.1x more than the Direct Burn's 17.0 kg. Divided by its own 180-day transit time, that is still only about 0.48 kg of deliverable payload per day — far below the Direct Burn's per-day figure — but the case's actual primary metric is kilograms of payload per day, not raw payload mass or raw speed alone, and a trajectory that delivers meaningfully more payload can in principle still win on that ratio if the extra payload outpaces the extra transit days by enough.
balance.margin_basis: Deliverable payload mass = wet mass (180 kg, sourced) minus dry mass (30 kg, stated Modeling Assumption MA4) minus propellant mass (derived via the rocket equation from each option's sourced/derived delta-v and Isp). Direct Burn: 180 - 30 - 133.0 = 17.0 kg deliverable payload, over a derived transit time of 0.221 days -> 76.9 kg/day. Patient Drift: 180 - 30 - 63.7 = 86.3 kg deliverable payload, over an assumed transit time of 180 days (MA3) -> 0.479 kg/day. The Direct Burn wins by roughly two orders of magnitude: its deliverable payload is only about 5x smaller than the Patient Drift's, but its transit time is about 800x shorter, so the ratio overwhelmingly favors speed. Appendix D's radiation-dose comparison against Appendix A's tolerance limit is a second, non-numeric-metric constraint (pass/fail against a stated tolerance, not itself part of the margin): both options pass under the sourced/assumed dose-rate figures (Direct Burn ~5.3 rad total; Patient Drift ~4,320 rad total, both well under the 20,000 rad tolerance), so the radiation check does not independently rule out either option here.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Payload customer's maximum acceptable delivery window
modeling_assumptions.basis: No public contract exists for the fictional Meridian Launch Systems. Anchored to real commercial precedent: satellite operators today routinely accept ~6-month (180-day) all-electric GTO-to-GEO transfers (Boeing 702SP / S8), so 240 days gives both options real, plausible headroom above the Patient Drift's own modeled 180-day transit.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Below 180 days, the Patient Drift becomes contractually unflyable outright regardless of the kg/day metric — the delivery-window constraint alone would decide the case. Above roughly 200 days it never binds either option.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Both trajectory options are modeled using the same geometric transfer ellipse (semi-major axis 24,521 km, eccentricity 0.7195)
modeling_assumptions.value_used: same a, e for both options
modeling_assumptions.basis: Both options genuinely start at the same real parking-orbit radius and are targeted to reach the same real GEO radius at apoapsis — the two-body ellipse connecting two fixed radii is geometrically unique. A real continuous low-thrust electric transfer does not actually trace a single Keplerian ellipse (it is a slowly-expanding spiral); modeling the Patient Drift as flying this same ellipse very slowly is a stated simplification for D1/D2 tractability, not a literal description of low-thrust dynamics.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Does not affect D3/D4/D5's mass or time economics, which are driven by delta-v, Isp, and transit time, not by the ellipse's shape. Only affects the D1/D2 parametric/rectangular-equation exercise, which becomes the same algebra for both options under this assumption — case-qa should consider whether a genuinely different geometry (e.g. a bi-elliptic transfer) would make D1/D2 more pedagogically distinct.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Patient Drift's modeled total transit time
modeling_assumptions.basis: Anchored to two real sources: commercial 702SP-class all-electric GTO-GEO transfers run ~6 months (S8), and Lozinski et al. 2019 documents electric orbit-raising transits of up to 200 days (S9). 180 days sits inside this real, published range.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: This is the single most consequential assumption in the case. D4's kg/day figure for the Patient Drift is inversely proportional to this number — halving it to 90 days would roughly double the Patient Drift's kg/day figure, but even doubling the Patient Drift's kg/day would not close the ~160x gap to the Direct Burn's kg/day figure (see balance.margin_basis).

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Kick stage dry (structure + engine + avionics) mass, fixed across both propulsion modes
modeling_assumptions.basis: No public figure exists for a single bus flying both a chemical and an electric mode at this delta-v/Isp combination (Sherpa-LTC and Sherpa-LTE are, in reality, separately-massed vehicles — see RESEARCH_LOG.md Key Finding #1). 30 kg is roughly 17% of the sourced 180 kg wet mass, a plausible structure-plus-avionics-plus-engine fraction for a small OTV.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Major lever. At dry mass >= 47.0 kg, the Direct Burn's deliverable payload mass drops to zero or negative — i.e. becomes physically infeasible under this chemical delta-v/Isp combination. Below that threshold, raising dry mass shrinks both options' payload roughly linearly, which narrows but does not come close to closing the ~160x kg/day gap to the Patient Drift.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Average radiation dose rate while actively within Van Allen belt-radius territory
modeling_assumptions.basis: No single dated, primary, apples-to-apples dose-rate figure could be found for this exact scenario (a fast chemical transit vs. a slow electric transit through the belts). Real published figures for related-but-different contexts ranged from roughly 200 to 3,700 rad/year depending on shielding thickness and orbital region — a genuinely shielding- and geometry-dependent figure, not a single settled number. 50 rad/day is a stated round mid-range value.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Patient Drift's cumulative dose scales directly with this rate: at the stated 50 rad/day it totals about 4,320 rad (well under the 20,000 rad tolerance, S10); at roughly 5x this rate (~250 rad/day) Patient Drift's dose would approach the tolerance ceiling and could flip the radiation check from pass to fail even though it does not change the kg/day comparison.

sensitivity_note: The primary-metric margin computed from sourced and derived figures is extreme (~15,900%, Direct Burn wins by roughly two orders of magnitude on kg/day) — see balance.margin_basis and FACILITATOR.md. This is flagged, not softened, per SPEC guidance: the case as currently specified is not a close call on the primary metric alone, and a retune (e.g. reconsidering MA3's transit time, MA4's dry mass, or whether kg/day is the right primary metric at all for this dilemma) should be considered before this case is treated as T2-appropriate 'close' case material. The radiation-dose check (Appendix D vs Appendix A) does not currently bind either option and does not rescue the balance.
